notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes for Luke 9:1–21, but there are three gaps. First, I found no Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan, Pentecostal or Orthodox comment on these verses. Second, I found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on them. Third, I found only a little from modern scholarship. The two places where readings really split are whether miracle power continues today (v. 2) and Peter's role (v. 20), but even there I have only one or two voices each.

Some sources are named only through other sites. NET Bible notes, Stein, Liefeld, Clarke and Barclay are quoted at preceptaustin.org or enduringword.com. Augustine and Bede come through Aquinas's *Catena Aurea* on Mark at ccel.org. I didn't read their own pages.

---

## Luke 9:1–21: Research notes

**v. 1**
- **Power and authority.** Two Greek words are used: *dunamis* means the ability to overcome, and *exousia* means the legal right. Luke used the same pair earlier, in 4:36, for Jesus' own exorcisms. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-9 (Utley)
- **The same idea from Steven Cole:** power is the ability to act, and authority is the right to use it. Only Jesus can hand both on to others. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-9-commentary
- **Demons and diseases are kept separate.** Precept Austin cites the NET Bible note, which says Luke distinguishes the two, so most illness isn't demonic. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-9-commentary
  - Guzik quotes Clarke: demons were cast out, diseases were healed. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
  - Utley agrees that the New Testament clearly separates demonic activity from physical illness. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-9
- **"Whom God calls, God equips."** Jesus called the Twelve and also gave them power to do the work. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **The Spirit as source.** The Holy Spirit isn't named here, but Precept Austin argues the Spirit was plainly the source of the apostles' power.
- **Judas.** Precept Austin notes that Judas probably shared this power too, which makes him more accountable. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-9-commentary
- **Text note.** Some manuscripts read "his disciples," "his twelve disciples" or "twelve apostles." The UBS4 Greek text rates "the Twelve" as almost certain. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-9

**v. 2**
- **"Sent" and "apostle" share a root** (*apostellō* and *apostolos*). Among the rabbis it meant an official representative sent with authority. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-9
  - Guzik, citing Pate, notes the same wordplay. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **The message.** The King has arrived, his kingdom is different from what people expected, and he gathers people who repent and believe. Preaching and healing go together. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **Kingdom of God.** This was the centre of Jesus' teaching. It is God's reign in hearts now, to be completed later over all the earth. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-9
- **Does miracle power continue today? (a point where views differ)**
  - Utley says God's power is still open to the church and the gifts are still active. But he says signs mainly confirm the gospel and its preacher. Where the gospel has taken root, believers should walk by faith and not demand miracles. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-9
  - Precept Austin applies the verse directly: every believer has the Spirit's power and should not try to minister without it. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-9-commentary
  - I found no Pentecostal or cessationist source treating this verse.
- **Matthew includes the "lost sheep of Israel" limit; Luke leaves it out.** Utley explains that each Gospel writer selected and adapted Jesus' words for his readers (Matthew for Jews, Luke for Gentiles), and says this is part of inspiration, not a breach of it. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-9

**v. 3**
- **Travelling light** kept the message simple and urgent and kept the disciples depending on God. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **Background.** Barclay cites a rabbinic rule against entering the Temple Mount with staff, shoes or money belt, to show you had left business behind. Josephus says the Essenes had similar travel rules (citing Pate). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **The bag.** Liefeld suggests the forbidden bag may be the kind travelling philosophers and religious beggars used to collect alms. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/

**v. 4**
- **Hospitality.** There were no inns to rely on, so the disciples depended on fellow Jews and learned that God provides for his workers. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61950/ 
- **NET note:** staying in one house set them apart from religious philosophers who went begging door to door. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61950/ 

**v. 5**
- **Shaking off dust.** Jews leaving a Gentile city often shook off its dust. Jesus was telling them to treat a Jewish town that rejected the message like a Gentile one. Their job was to present the message persuasively, not to force a change of mind. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/

**v. 6**
- **Obedience.** They did what Jesus said, with both the mission and the power to carry it out. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/

**vv. 7–8**
- **Herod.** This is Herod Antipas. Guzik sees no sincere spiritual interest in him, and says his guilty conscience over John added to his confusion. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **The popular opinions:**
  - John: a herald calling the nation to repent.
  - Elijah: a miracle worker, promised to return in Malachi 4:5–6.
  - "A prophet of old": perhaps the prophet Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15–19. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **Older Catholic/patristic view.** Augustine, quoted in Aquinas's *Catena Aurea*, says Luke shows that others, not Herod himself, claimed John had risen. Luke pictures Herod as unsure. — https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena2.iii.vi.html 

**v. 9**
- **Herod wanted to see Jesus** out of curiosity or hostility, not as a real seeker. Luke later shows him wanting to kill Jesus (13:32) and mocking him at the trial. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **A sermon on preceptaustin.org** says Herod asked the right question, but he never answered it correctly. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-sermons

**v. 10**
- **"Disciples" become "apostles."** Learners when they left, they come back as messengers sent with authority. Jesus then takes them aside to care for them. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **Where was Bethsaida?** Bede, in the *Catena*, says Luke means the deserted country belonging to Bethsaida, not the town itself. — https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena2.iii.vi.html 

**v. 11**
- **Three ways Jesus served the crowd:**
  - he welcomed them (his attitude);
  - he taught about the kingdom;
  - he healed. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/

**vv. 12–13**
- **The disciples' suggestion.** They probably couldn't imagine a miracle, so sending the crowd away seemed kind. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **"You give them something to eat"** tested both their faith and their compassion. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **Lowell Johnson** reads it as Jesus telling the men who had just reported great deeds to now feed the people. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons-luke-lowell-johnson 

**vv. 14–15**
- **Groups of fifty.** This made the meal orderly and festive, like a banquet. It also made the crowd easier to count, which supports the figure of 5,000 men. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **Application:** the disciples simply did as Jesus told them. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61950/ 

**v. 16**
- **"Blessed."** Jesus blessed (thanked) God for the food; he didn't bless the food itself. He did the miracle through the disciples' hands. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **Precept Austin** says Jesus was doing what every Jewish father did at a meal, showing God as the source of all provision. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61950/ 
- **Catholic reading: the Eucharist**
  - catholic.com cites the Catechism (CCC 1335): the feedings prefigure the superabundance of this unique bread of his Eucharist. — https://www.catholic.com/qa/was-jesus-feeding-of-the-5000-really-a-miracle-of-sharing
  - Another catholic.com piece points to the same pattern of words in the feedings and the Last Supper: Jesus takes, blesses, breaks and gives. — https://www.catholic.com/audio/caf/the-mass-in-the-early-church 
  - A third argues that the loaves multiplied as the disciples handed them out. On this view the miracle prepares believers for the Eucharist, where the substance changes but the bread's quantity stays the same. — https://www.catholic.com/audio/scw/does-remembrance-refute-the-real-presence-a-catholic-response 
  - It also stresses that the apostles were intermediaries between Christ and the people. — https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/will-you-also-go-away-0 
- **The "miracle of sharing" view.** Some modern readers say the crowd shared hidden food after Jesus set the example. catholic.com describes this view and rejects it. — https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/will-you-also-go-away-0 
  - It also states plainly that the feeding was a genuine, supernatural miracle that could not have been accomplished by any natural means. — https://www.catholic.com/qa/was-jesus-feeding-of-the-5000-really-a-miracle-of-sharing

**v. 17**
- **Jesus is greater than earlier prophets.** Elisha fed a hundred men with some left over (2 Kings 4:42–44), and Moses' people were fed in the wilderness. Jesus exceeds both. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **Early Christian art.** Loaves and fishes appear on catacomb walls. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
  - catholic.com says this was the earliest and always the favorite symbol of the Eucharist in early Christian monuments. — https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/early-symbols-of-the-eucharist
- **Leftovers.** Guzik says Jesus "knew that wastefulness didn't glorify the God of all provision." Another note contrasts the manna, which had no edible leftovers. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61950/ 
- **Morgan's application:** servants give Jesus all they have and obey him, even when worldly prudence objects. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/

**v. 18**
- **Prayer.** The scene opens with Jesus praying. It is unclear whether the disciples prayed with him or interrupted him. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/ 

**v. 19**
- **The same three guesses as vv. 7–8.** Elijah is linked to the Messianic kingdom (Malachi 4:5), and "one of the prophets" may mean the Prophet of Deuteronomy 18. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-9 
- **Guzik:** seeing Jesus as John or Elijah may show hope for a political messiah. — https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Luk/Luk_9.cfm 

**v. 20**
- **"You" is plural and emphatic,** so the question is put to all the disciples. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-9 
- **"The Christ of God"** means God's Messiah, the Messiah from the heart of God, *not* the Messiah from the desire of man. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **Gill:** Peter speaks for all, with the others agreeing. Gill notes that the Persian version reads "Christ God." — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-20.html 
- **Liefeld (via Cole):** this is the first time a disciple calls Jesus Messiah, a turning point in Luke. — https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-42-crucial-question-luke-918-22 
- **Right title, wrong picture:**
  - Peter's answer was right, but he pictured a reigning king. Cole adds that this is quite correct when understood of Messiah's second coming, a premillennial reading. — https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-42-crucial-question-luke-918-22
  - Utley says the disciples' idea of Messiah came more from rabbinic Judaism than from Jesus. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-9 
- **Why does Luke leave out "Son of the living God"?** Constable suggests that for Luke's Gentile readers, "Christ" already meant a divine Messiah. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-20.html 
- **Peter's role (a point where views differ):**
  - Ellicott's commentary (an Anglican-era work) notes that Luke omits Jesus' blessing of Peter. It says that blessing can have conferred on him no sort of primacy or superior authority among the Apostles. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/9-20.htm
  - The biblehub.com study notes say Peter's confession becomes a cornerstone for the early church's understanding, coming by divine revelation. — https://biblehub.com/luke/9-20.htm
  - I found no Catholic source on this verse itself.
- **Expositor's Greek Testament (older critical scholarship):** Luke's wording speaks the language of the apostolic age. Mark's shorter form is more original by comparison. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/9-20.htm

**v. 21**
- **Stein: why the silence?** The command came not because Peter's confession was false but precisely because it was true. Telling the public would have been dangerous, because to them "Messiah" meant a king who would throw off Rome, while to Jesus it meant suffering. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-9-commentary 
- **William Kelly:** there was no use proclaiming him Messiah, because despite prophecy, miracles and preaching the people had got it wrong. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-20.html 
- **Guzik:** Jesus immediately goes on (v. 22) to reveal that the Son of Man must suffer and die, something the disciples couldn't grasp until after the resurrection. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
